items.originalTitle: EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has released EmbeddingGemma 2, an open-source multimodal embedding model designed for efficient on-device inference across text, images, audio, and video. With 740 million parameters and built on the Gemma 4 architecture, the model supports unified embedding spaces for various data types and is optimized for resource-constrained hardware, enabling privacy-preserving and low-latency applications.

EmbeddingGemma 2 improves code embedding performance significantly and matches or outperforms larger models on multiple benchmarks while offering modularity and storage efficiency through dynamic vector truncation. It supports an extended 8K token context window and integrates with generative models like Gemma 4 to facilitate on-device retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipelines. The model is available under an Apache 2.0 license with weights accessible on Hugging Face and Kaggle.

items.title: OpenTPU launches open-source AI accelerator designed by AI, running multiple modern models on FPGA with bit-exact simulation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenTPU – An open-source AI accelerator, developed by AI
items.summary:
OpenTPU is an open-source AI accelerator project developed using AI to design hardware that runs its own inference. It includes a complete hardware design, instruction set, simulator, compiler, and host software, enabling users to understand AI accelerator internals from hardware to software. The accelerator runs ten modern AI models on an FPGA card, producing bit-for-bit identical outputs to its simulator, demonstrating practical performance and accuracy.

The design operates on a Xilinx Kintex-7 FPGA with DDR3 memory, supporting models up to 35 billion parameters using mixture-of-experts techniques with expert data streamed from host storage. It uses 4-bit and int8 quantization to optimize memory and speed, achieving up to 45% faster decoding speeds with minimal accuracy loss. The project serves both as a functional AI accelerator and a learning resource for hardware and software integration in AI systems.

items.summary:
OpenAI has introduced the Decisions API in public beta, offering about 10 times faster evaluation of text, images, or both compared to its Responses API. The API returns typed answers such as probabilities, choices from fixed sets, or scores against rubrics, enabling applications to classify content, route requests, and prioritize work more efficiently.

The Decisions API uses the gpt-6-luna model and supports predicate, choice, and score question types to assess conditions, select categories, or rate ordered levels. It accepts combined text and base64-encoded images as input and provides probability estimates to guide automated decisions. OpenAI expects to move the API to general availability in the coming weeks.

items.title: Utah allows AI to examine patients and prescribe acne medication without direct doctor oversight in a limited one-year pilot [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Utah to let AI examine patients and prescribe medication without human oversight
items.summary:
Utah has launched a one-year pilot program permitting a healthcare startup, Nolla Health, to use AI to examine patients with mild-to-moderate acne and prescribe medication without direct human oversight. The program starts with AI analyzing patient-submitted facial scans and medical histories to recommend treatments from a list of eight approved topical medications.

The pilot includes phased oversight: the first 100 prescriptions require doctor review before pharmacy submission, the next 400 prescriptions are submitted by AI with weekly retrospective physician review, and thereafter doctors review at least 10% of prescriptions monthly. The program aims to explore AI's role in treating less serious conditions while limiting risks associated with AI medical advice.

items.summary:
Epoch.ai analyzed AI performance benchmarks from the past three years and found that the cost to achieve a given level of AI capability has dropped about 47% per quarter, or 13 times per year, since 2023. This rate of decline is significantly faster than historical price drops in technologies like DNA sequencing, computing, lithium batteries, and electricity. The study highlights that price reductions vary by domain, with math problems seeing faster cost declines than game-based puzzles, and that prices fall most rapidly immediately after a new performance level is first achieved.

The analysis is based on five AI benchmarks covering mathematics, hard sciences, and games of skill, and includes data such as OpenAI's GPT models reducing the cost per question on a PhD-level science exam by over 700 times in under 18 months. The report notes caveats including potential benchmark-specific training and differences between benchmark performance and real-world utility. Despite these limitations, the findings suggest that the "price of thought" in AI is decreasing at an unprecedented pace compared to other general-purpose technologies.

The report notes caveats including potential benchmark-specific training and differences between benchmark performance and real-world utility. Despite these limitations, the findings suggest that the "price of thought" in AI is decreasing at an unprecedented pace compared to other general-purpose technologies.

items.originalTitle: EmbeddingGemma 2
items.summary:
My comment on EmbeddingGemma 2 — Hacker News.

I really appreciate that EmbeddingGemma 2 is under the Apache 2.0 license.

For embedding models in particular, I don't think it makes sense to use a closed, proprietary, hosted-only model.

Most applications of embedding models involve calculating thousands or even millions of embedding vectors and storing them for later comparison.

If your model is proprietary, the vendor is likely someday going to decide to stop offering that model. They'll have a better model to replace it, but you still need to pay to re-calculate those millions of stored existing vectors.

(In April 2024 OpenAI offered to "cover the financial cost of users re-embedding content with these new models" - https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-api-general-availability/ - but I don't think that's something we can rely on from every provider.)

Notably, I don't want to host the model myself. I'd much rather pay a provider for a hosted model while knowing that if they ever stop hosting it I can run the open weights version myself - or find another vendor who can do that for me.

items.originalTitle: Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk
items.summary:
Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk

Mistral are back in the game. Today they're releasing a preview of Mistral Large 4, a 1 trillion parameter, 49 billion active parameter model trained on their own cluster of 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs.

The preview is available via their API. They promise to release the open weights model at the "end of this month".

The model only supports two reasoning levels - "none" and "high" - via the Mistral API. Here are both pelicans - the "high" one looks better, though surprisingly it only used 2,717 output tokens compared to "none" which used 3,275:

On Artificial Analysis it scores 38, just behind DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, which is a 552B model. It's a huge improvement on last December's Mistral Large 3, which drew this terrible pelican and scored 9 on AA.

It's certainly not a Fable-class model, but it's great to see Mistral put out a model that's back to being maybe about 6 months behind the frontier.

Via Hacker News

items.originalTitle: AI Whistleblowers Say Researchers Are Checking AI Less Frequently
items.summary:
It won’t be any surprise to people with human intelligence that Monday’s New York City Council hearing on the risks of AI was as theatrical as a Broadway show. What was more surprising was what the AI researchers testified about how AI research is evolving, and what that means for their job.

For those who missed it, the city council heard testimony from three AI lab whistleblowers: Jacob Coxon, formerly of Anthropic and OpenAI; Alex Turner, formerly of Google DeepMind; and Daniel Kokotajlo, formerly of OpenAI. Afterwards, they heard from representatives of the AI labs. We’ll get to that lower down.

One of the most interesting parts of the whistleblowers’ testimony related to the AI research process. Coxon and Kokotajlo each said that researchers at the labs have lately been letting AI drive the process of writing code and research. Researchers check AI’s work less frequently, they said.

The labs might not agree with that exact characterization, although their representatives weren’t asked about it at the hearing. But the labs have been the first to say that AI has greatly accelerated the process of AI research. Anthropic even said in a report last month that, as of August, AI was leading more than a quarter of model research and development at the company.
